questions.question: A steady current of 0.40 A flows in a metal wire. How many electrons pass a point in the wire each second? A 2.5 x 10^18, B 6.4 x 10^-20, C 4.0 x 10^-19, D 2.5 x 10^19
steps: Current = charge per second, so I = N e / t, where N / t is the number of electrons passing per second.
B is I x e and C is e / I; D has the wrong power of ten.

questions.question: A uniform metal wire has resistance R. The wire is stretched to twice its original length without any change of volume or of resistivity. What is the new resistance of the wire? A R/2, B R, C 2R, D 4R
steps: The volume is constant, so doubling the length halves the cross-sectional area.
R = rho L / A, so the new resistance is rho (2L) / (A / 2) = 4 rho L / A = 4R.
B ignores the change of area; C allows for the length only; A inverts the effect of the length (R/2).

questions.question: The resistance of the filament of a lamp increases as the current through it increases. Explain this, in terms of the behaviour of the electrons and the metal ions in the filament.
questions.answer: A greater current heats the filament, so the metal ions vibrate with a larger amplitude. The electrons collide with the ions more often, so for a given p.d. their drift velocity and the current are smaller, and the resistance V / I is greater.
steps: A greater current heats the filament, so its temperature rises and the metal ions vibrate with greater amplitude.
The conduction electrons collide with the ions more frequently, so their mean drift velocity for a given p.d. is smaller.
The current increases less than in proportion to the p.d., so the ratio V / I (the resistance) increases.
accept: The number of free electrons per unit volume in a metal stays approximately constant, so the change is due to the collisions.
More collisions per second mean a smaller mean time between collisions for the electrons.
The resistivity of a metal increases with temperature.

questions.question: A heating coil is to be made from nichrome wire of diameter 0.28 mm. The resistivity of nichrome is 1.1 x 10^-6 ohm m. Calculate the length of wire needed to make a resistance of 12 ohm.
steps: Cross-sectional area A = pi (0.14 x 10^-3)^2 = 6.16 x 10^-8 m^2.
R = rho L / A, so L = R A / rho.

questions.question: A copper wire of diameter 1.2 mm carries a current of 3.5 A. The number of free electrons per unit volume in copper is 8.5 x 10^28 m^-3. Calculate the mean drift velocity of the electrons.
steps: Cross-sectional area A = pi (0.60 x 10^-3)^2 = 1.13 x 10^-6 m^2.
I = n A v e, so v = I / (n A e).

questions.question: The heating element of a toaster is a nichrome wire of length 4.2 m and diameter 0.40 mm. At its working temperature the resistivity of nichrome is 1.1 x 10^-6 ohm m. Calculate the resistance of the element at this temperature.

The heating element of a toaster is a nichrome wire that has a resistance of 37 ohm at its working temperature. It is connected to a 230 V supply. Using the resistance of 37 ohm from part (a), calculate the power dissipated in the element.

The heating element of a toaster is a nichrome wire of length 4.2 m and diameter 0.40 mm, and it dissipates 1.4 x 10^3 W on a 230 V supply. The resistivity of nichrome at the working temperature is 1.1 x 10^-6 ohm m. The element is replaced by one of the same length and material but with a diameter of 0.50 mm. Assume that the resistivity is unchanged. Calculate the power dissipated in the new element on the 230 V supply, and explain why it is different from 1.4 x 10^3 W.
questions.answer: Power = 2.2 x 10^3 W. The thicker wire has a smaller resistance, so with the same p.d. the current and the power are greater.
steps: New area A = pi (0.25 x 10^-3)^2 = 1.96 x 10^-7 m^2, so R = rho L / A = 23.5 ohm.
The larger area gives a smaller resistance, so for the same p.d. the current is larger and P = V^2 / R is greater (by a factor of 1.6).

questions.question: A 12 ohm resistor and a 6.0 ohm resistor are connected in parallel. This combination is connected in series with a 5.0 ohm resistor. What is the total resistance of the circuit? A 2.2 ohm, B 9.0 ohm, C 15 ohm, D 23 ohm
steps: The parallel pair: 1 / R = 1/12 + 1/6 = 1/4, so R = 4.0 ohm.
In series with 5.0 ohm: total = 4.0 + 5.0 = 9.0 ohm.
A treats all three as parallel; C pairs the 6.0 ohm and 5.0 ohm in parallel and adds the 12 ohm; D adds all three in series.

questions.question: A cell of e.m.f. 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.50 ohm is connected across a resistor of resistance 2.5 ohm. What is the potential difference across the resistor? A 0.25 V, B 1.0 V, C 1.25 V, D 1.5 V
steps: p.d. across the resistor = I R = 0.50 x 2.5 = 1.25 V (equivalently E - I r = 1.5 - 0.25).
A is the p.d. across the internal resistance; B is E - r; D ignores the internal resistance.

questions.question: Explain why the terminal potential difference of a battery decreases as the current drawn from the battery increases.
questions.answer: The battery has internal resistance r. The terminal p.d. is V = E - I r, where E is constant, so a larger current gives a larger p.d. lost across the internal resistance and a smaller terminal p.d.
steps: The battery has an internal resistance r, and its e.m.f. E is constant.
The p.d. lost across the internal resistance is I r, so it increases when the current I increases.
The terminal p.d. V = E - I r, so V decreases as I increases.
accept: Lost volts = E - V.
More energy per unit charge is transferred inside the battery when the current is larger.
A graph of terminal p.d. against current has gradient -r.

questions.question: A potential divider is made from a fixed resistor of resistance 5.0 kohm in series with a negative temperature coefficient (NTC) thermistor, connected across a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. The output p.d. is taken across the fixed resistor. At 60 degrees C the resistance of the thermistor is 3.4 kohm. Calculate the output p.d. at 60 degrees C. Explain why the output p.d. is greater at 60 degrees C than at 20 degrees C, when the resistance of the thermistor is 12 kohm.
questions.answer: Output p.d. at 60 degrees C = 3.6 V. The thermistor resistance falls as the temperature rises, so a smaller share of the supply p.d. is across the thermistor and a larger share is across the fixed resistor.
steps: Output p.d. = supply p.d. x R / (R + R_thermistor) = 6.0 x 5.0 / (5.0 + 3.4).
The resistance of an NTC thermistor decreases as the temperature rises.
The thermistor takes a smaller share of the 6.0 V supply, so the p.d. across the fixed resistor increases (it is 1.76 V at 20 degrees C).
accept: The p.d.s across the two resistors add up to 6.0 V, so a smaller p.d. across the thermistor means a larger p.d. across the fixed resistor.
The total resistance falls, so the current increases and the p.d. I R across the fixed resistor increases.
Output at 20 degrees C = 6.0 x 5.0 / (5.0 + 12) = 1.76 V, which is less than at 60 degrees C.

questions.question: A cell supplies a current of 0.30 A when the potential difference across its terminals is 1.35 V. When the current is 0.80 A the terminal potential difference is 1.20 V. Determine the e.m.f. and the internal resistance of the cell.
steps: Terminal p.d. V = E - I r for each reading.
Subtracting: 0.15 = 0.50 r, so r = 0.30 ohm.

questions.question: A battery has e.m.f. 9.0 V and internal resistance 1.5 ohm. It is connected to a circuit in which a 6.0 ohm resistor and a 3.0 ohm resistor in parallel are in series with a 2.5 ohm resistor. Show that the total resistance of the circuit, including the internal resistance of the battery, is 6.0 ohm.
steps: Parallel pair: 1 / R = 1/6.0 + 1/3.0 = 1/2.0, so R = 2.0 ohm.

questions.question: A battery has e.m.f. 9.0 V and internal resistance 1.5 ohm. It is connected to a circuit in which a 6.0 ohm resistor and a 3.0 ohm resistor in parallel are in series with a 2.5 ohm resistor. Calculate the current in the 3.0 ohm resistor.
questions.answer: Current in the 3.0 ohm resistor = 1.0 A
steps: Current from the battery I = E / R_total = 9.0 / 6.0 = 1.5 A.
P.d. across the parallel pair = I x 2.0 = 3.0 V.
Current in the 3.0 ohm resistor = 3.0 / 3.0 = 1.0 A.

questions.question: A battery has e.m.f. 9.0 V and internal resistance 1.5 ohm. It is connected to a circuit in which a 6.0 ohm resistor and a 3.0 ohm resistor in parallel are in series with a 2.5 ohm resistor. A student says that the percentage of the total power of the battery that is delivered to the external circuit increases if the 2.5 ohm resistor is replaced by a 5.0 ohm resistor. Calculate the percentage of the total power delivered to the external circuit in the original circuit, and decide whether the student is correct.
questions.answer: Original: 75% delivered to the external circuit. With the 5.0 ohm resistor it is 82%, so the student is correct.
steps: Total power = E I = 9.0 x 1.5 = 13.5 W; power in internal resistance = I^2 r = 3.38 W.
Power delivered to the external circuit = 13.5 - 3.38 = 10.1 W, which is 75% of the total.
In general the percentage is R_ext / (R_ext + r) x 100, since the same current flows in all the resistance.
With a 5.0 ohm resistor R_ext = 7.0 ohm, giving 7.0 / 8.50 x 100 = 82%, which is greater, so the student is correct.

questions.question: A 470 uF capacitor is charged until the potential difference across it is 12 V. How much energy is stored in the capacitor? A 2.8 x 10^-3 J, B 5.6 x 10^-3 J, C 3.4 x 10^-2 J, D 6.8 x 10^-2 J
steps: A is 1/2 C V, B is C V (the charge, in coulombs) and D is C V^2, which omits the factor 1/2.

questions.question: A capacitor discharges through a resistor in a circuit of time constant 4.0 s. The initial charge on the capacitor is Q0. What is the charge on the capacitor 8.0 s after the discharge begins? A 0.14 Q0, B 0.37 Q0, C 0.50 Q0, D 0.018 Q0
steps: B is the value after one time constant, C assumes the charge halves in each time constant, and D uses e^-4.

questions.question: A capacitor, a resistor and a cell of constant e.m.f. are connected in series with a switch. The capacitor is initially uncharged. Explain why the current in the circuit falls to zero some time after the switch is closed, even though the cell remains connected.
questions.answer: Charge flows on to the plates, so the p.d. across the capacitor rises. The p.d. across the resistor (E - V_C) falls, so the current falls. When the capacitor p.d. equals the e.m.f. there is no p.d. across the resistor, so the current is zero.
steps: Initially the capacitor p.d. is zero, so the whole e.m.f. is across the resistor and the current is E / R.
As charge flows on to the plates the capacitor p.d. rises, so the p.d. across the resistor (E - V_C) falls and the current falls.
When the capacitor p.d. equals the e.m.f. there is no p.d. across the resistor, so the current is zero.
accept: Charge cannot cross the gap between the plates, so there is a current only while the capacitor is charging.
The current decreases exponentially with time.
The capacitor p.d. V_C = Q / C increases as the charge Q on the plates increases.

questions.question: A 2200 uF capacitor charged to a potential difference of 9.0 V discharges through a 4.7 kohm resistor. Calculate the time taken for the potential difference across the capacitor to fall to 3.0 V.
steps: Time constant RC = 4.7 x 10^3 x 2200 x 10^-6 = 10.34 s.

questions.question: The flash unit of a camera contains a 180 uF capacitor that is charged to 330 V. When the flash fires, all of the stored energy is transferred in 2.0 ms. Calculate the energy stored by the capacitor and the mean power of the flash.
steps: Mean power = energy / time = 9.80 / 2.0 x 10^-3 = 4.90 x 10^3 W.
So the energy is 9.8 J and the mean power is 4.9 kW.

questions.question: A capacitor is charged to a potential difference V0 and then discharged through a resistor of resistance R. The potential difference V across the capacitor at time t is given by V = V0 e^(-t / RC), where C is the capacitance. Show that a graph of ln V against t is a straight line, and state what its gradient is equal to.
questions.answer: ln V = ln V0 - t / (RC), which has the form y = m x + c, so the graph is a straight line with gradient -1 / (RC).
steps: Take natural logarithms of V = V0 e^(-t / RC) to give ln V = ln V0 + ln(e^(-t / RC)).
This simplifies to ln V = ln V0 - t / (RC).
Comparing with y = m x + c, a graph of ln V against t is a straight line with gradient -1 / (RC) and intercept ln V0.
accept: Using log to base 10 instead gives a straight line with gradient -0.434 / (RC).
The intercept on the ln V axis is ln V0.

questions.question: A capacitor is discharged through a resistor of resistance 47 kohm. The potential difference V across the capacitor obeys V = V0 e^(-t / RC), and the gradient of the graph of ln V against t (with V in volts and t in seconds) is -0.0238 s^-1. Calculate the capacitance of the capacitor.
steps: The magnitude of the gradient = 1 / (RC), so C = 1 / (gradient x R).

questions.question: A capacitor is marked 1000 uF with a tolerance of +/- 10%. It is discharged through a 47 kohm resistor, and the graph of ln V against t has a gradient of -0.0238 s^-1 with an uncertainty of +/- 0.0007 s^-1. Evaluate whether the experimental value of the capacitance is consistent with the marked value.
questions.answer: The result ranges from 868 uF to 921 uF, which overlaps the allowed range of 900 uF to 1100 uF, so the result is consistent with the marked value (although the best value of 894 uF is slightly below 900 uF).
steps: The marked range is 1000 +/- 10%, i.e. 900 uF to 1100 uF.
Using the uncertainty in the gradient (0.0245 and 0.0231 s^-1), C ranges from 868 uF to 921 uF.
The best value (894 uF) is just below the tolerance range, but the ranges overlap (900 uF to 921 uF), so the result is consistent with the marked value within the experimental uncertainty.
accept: Percentage uncertainty in the gradient is 2.9%, so C = 894 +/- 26 uF.
The experiment cannot show that the capacitor is outside its tolerance.
More readings, or a more precise gradient, would be needed to decide.

questions.question: A horizontal straight wire of length 0.15 m lies in an east-west direction and carries a current of 3.0 A towards the east. It is in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.20 T that is directed vertically upwards. What is the force on the wire? A 0.090 N towards the north, B 0.60 N towards the north, C 0.60 N towards the south, D 0.090 N towards the south
steps: The wire is at right angles to the field, so F = B I L = 0.20 x 3.0 x 0.15 = 0.090 N.
By Fleming's left-hand rule (field upwards, current to the east) the force is horizontal and towards the south.
B and C omit the length of the wire; A has the correct size but the opposite direction.

questions.question: A coil of 200 turns has the magnetic flux through each turn reduced uniformly from 4.0 mWb to zero in 0.25 s. What is the magnitude of the average e.m.f. induced in the coil? A 0.016 V, B 3.2 V, C 0.80 V, D 3.2 x 10^3 V
steps: Induced e.m.f. = N x change in flux / time = 200 x 4.0 x 10^-3 / 0.25 = 3.2 V.
A omits the number of turns; C omits the time; D uses 4.0 Wb instead of 4.0 mWb.

questions.question: A straight metal rod is pulled at constant speed along two horizontal conducting rails that are connected at one end through a resistor. There is a uniform vertical magnetic field. Explain why a constant horizontal force must be applied to the rod to keep it moving at constant speed.
questions.answer: The moving rod changes the magnetic flux through the circuit, so an e.m.f. and current are induced. The current-carrying rod in the field experiences a force that opposes its motion (Lenz's law), so an equal and opposite applied force is needed for zero resultant force.
steps: The moving rod changes the flux linkage with the circuit, so an e.m.f. is induced and a current flows in the circuit.
The current-carrying rod in the magnetic field experiences a force which, by Lenz's law, opposes the motion of the rod.
For constant speed the resultant force must be zero, so an applied force equal and opposite to the magnetic force is needed.
accept: Conservation of energy: the work done by the applied force is transferred as thermal energy in the circuit.
The magnetic force on the rod is B I L, where I is the induced current.
If the circuit were broken there would be no current and no magnetic force to overcome.

questions.question: An electron moving at 4.0 x 10^6 m s^-1 enters a region of uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.80 mT. The velocity of the electron is at right angles to the field. Calculate the radius of the circular path of the electron.
steps: The magnetic force B e v provides the centripetal force: B e v = m v^2 / r.
r = m v / (B e).

questions.question: Two coils are wound on the same soft iron core. An alternating current in the primary coil produces an alternating e.m.f. in the secondary coil. Explain how this happens, and why no e.m.f. is induced in the secondary coil if the primary coil is connected to a steady direct current.
questions.answer: The alternating current produces a changing magnetic flux in the core, which links the secondary coil, so the flux linkage in the secondary changes and an e.m.f. is induced (Faraday's law). A steady direct current gives a constant flux, so there is no change of flux linkage and no e.m.f.
steps: The alternating current in the primary coil produces a magnetic flux that changes continuously.
The soft iron core links this flux with the secondary coil, so the flux linkage in the secondary changes continuously.
By Faraday's law an e.m.f. proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage is induced in the secondary coil.
A steady direct current gives a constant flux, so there is no change of flux linkage and no e.m.f. is induced.
accept: The iron core concentrates the flux so that nearly all of it links both coils.
Lenz's law gives the direction of the induced e.m.f.
The e.m.f. induced is N d(Phi) / dt, where N is the number of turns on the secondary coil.

questions.question: A simple generator has a rectangular coil of 120 turns, each of area 4.5 x 10^-3 m^2. The coil rotates in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.065 T. Calculate the maximum flux linkage of the coil.
questions.answer: Maximum flux linkage = 3.5 x 10^-2 Wb (3.51 x 10^-2 Wb before rounding)
steps: The flux linkage is greatest when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field: N Phi = N B A.

keywords: rate of change of flux linkage
questions.question: A simple generator has a rectangular coil of 120 turns, each of area 4.5 x 10^-3 m^2, rotating at 8.0 revolutions per second in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.065 T. Calculate the mean e.m.f. induced while the coil turns from the position where its plane is perpendicular to the field to the position where its plane is parallel to the field.
questions.answer: Mean e.m.f. = 1.1 V (1.12 V before rounding)
steps: This is a quarter of a revolution, so the time taken is (1 / 8.0) / 4 = 0.03125 s.
The flux linkage falls from 3.51 x 10^-2 Wb to zero.
Mean e.m.f. = change in flux linkage / time = 3.51 x 10^-2 / 0.03125 = 1.12 V, i.e. 1.1 V.

questions.question: A simple generator has a rectangular coil of 120 turns, each of area 4.5 x 10^-3 m^2, rotating at 8.0 revolutions per second in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.065 T. The mean e.m.f. while the coil turns from perpendicular to parallel to the field is 1.12 V. The coil is now rotated at twice the original rate. State and explain how this affects the frequency of the e.m.f. and the mean e.m.f. during the same quarter of a revolution.
questions.answer: The frequency doubles. The same change of flux linkage happens in half the time, so the mean e.m.f. doubles to 2.24 V.
steps: The frequency of the e.m.f. doubles (twice as many revolutions per second).
The same change of flux linkage in a quarter turn now takes half the time.
Induced e.m.f. = rate of change of flux linkage, so the mean e.m.f. doubles, to 2 x 1.12 = 2.24 V.
accept: The peak e.m.f. also doubles, since it is proportional to the angular speed.
The period of the alternating e.m.f. halves.
The maximum flux linkage N B A is unchanged.
